title_original: Images Vevey: Families, I Love You
excerpt_original: “Families, I hate you!” thundered André Gide in 1897, in Fruits of the Earth. More than a century later, on the shore of Lake Geneva, the sentiment has flipped. Families, I love you, then, and set to music: for the tenth edition of the biennial he founded in 2008, Stefano Stoll…

blocks.text: “Families, I hate you!” thundered André Gide in 1897, in Fruits of the Earth . More than a century later, on the shore of Lake Geneva, the sentiment has flipped. Families, I love you, then, and set to music: for the tenth edition of the biennial he founded in 2008, Stefano Stoll drew his theme from Sister Sledge, “We Are Family,” the obligatory soundtrack of weddings and christenings, which entered the Grammy Hall of Fame the very year Images Vevey was born (fate has a sense of humor). Beneath the disco ball, an idea. “It’s precisely within families that you learn nuance, that you learn to live together”, the director argues, “to get worked up at the uncle who isn’t on your side of the political fence at Christmas.” By March, he adds, you can see him again, at the cousin’s wedding. A lesson in domestic diplomacy.

Visitors stepping off the train are met at once by a familiar face. On Place de la Gare, Martin Parr sits among the flowers, while behind him Alice, the daughter of Siân Davey, waves a balloon. The English photographer, who died in December 2025, appears in “The Garden”, Siân Davey’s series about a wild garden opened to neighbors, loved ones and passersby. An elegant detour, dictated by house rule: Images Vevey shows only living artists. “We’ve never done deceased people, we’ve never done what would have made life easier for us, certainly”, Stefano Stoll admits. “But we like complicated things.” Martin Parr, who never missed a chance to sing the biennial’s praises, would surely have relished the twist.

On the Grande Place, between the Grenette and the Bois d’Amour, Barbara Davatz unfurls an open-air family tree. A masterwork of patience. In 1982, in a Zurich still electrified by youth riots, the Swiss photographer, born in 1944, had 12 couples of lovers, friends or relatives pose in her studio, facing the camera against a plain grey backdrop, shot on a large-format camera in black and white. She started again in 1988, in 1997 and in 2014, with the same subjects, their new partners, their children, soon their grandchildren. Three generations, 14 children swelling the ranks, couples forming and dissolving, hairstyles that date each decade more reliably than carbon-14. The protocol stays identical; only the faces change. Davatz calls it her “photographic family”, and this year, the phrase lands perfectly. “Every picture is the record of a relationship, the sum of the pictures is a record of time”, the artist sums up. A record you walk through here in a few steps, decade to decade, scanning the faces for who stayed, who left, who arrived.

Back toward the station, in the former railway workers’ housing, L’Appartement lives up to its name. Richard Billingham marks the 30th anniversary of Ray’s a Laugh , published in 1996 by the Zurich publisher Walter Keller (Scalo), a book Stefano Stoll discovered in London in 1997, at the “Sensation” exhibition, where his parents had taken him. In the family, inevitably. “All of a sudden I understood that Richard’s parents, Liz and Ray, actually lived in two separate apartments”, he recalls. Two towers of the same council estate, in Margaret Thatcher’s England. Liz leaves with Jason, the younger brother; Ray stays with Richard for four years, living on his notorious “home-brewed beer”, until she agrees to take him back, the alcoholic, on condition that he stops drinking. The show follows that geography: on one side, Liz’s flat; on the other, Ray’s, where unpublished black-and-white prints show one man and his room. Further on, the film Fishtank (1998) plays in a room wallpapered to match. “We were like fish in a tank”, Richard Billingham once told the director, who draws his own moral from it: “We, in our tidy Swiss households, learn to live with very little chaos. In the end, chaos is life.”

At Château de l’Aile, where not a single nail is allowed, Vik Muniz reassembles, from thousands of photographs picked up at flea markets, everything a family album contains: the children’s birthdays, the parents’ wedding, mom at the beach, the first bike. A few rooms further, a change of dynasty. In the room next door, Cristina De Middel, whose very first exhibition took place in Vevey back in 2010, hangs “Endofgamia”, a title that fuses endogamy and endgame. It began as a Prado commission: the artist selected the royal-family galleries, the Spanish Habsburgs first among them, and superimposed the portraits, keeping the eyes in the same place. “It created a kind of monster where you can still recognize the family’s distinctive features”, she says (the Habsburg chin has never looked so collective). The museum balked. “They didn’t like it”, De Middel recalls, “because it was a bit critical of the royal family, and we were in a kingdom, after all.” Printed on a metallic, reflective surface, these hybrid faces seem to follow visitors with their gaze, as in a haunted château. “If you don’t like the show, it’s too late now, Cristina”, Stefano Stoll tells the artist, freshly arrived from Brazil to discover an installation designed remotely. Family humor.

Time passing, again. At the Musée de la Confrérie des Vignerons, guardian of a festival held every 25 years, “once a generation”, Rineke Dijkstra, a fixture of the world’s great museums, agreed to be shown “in pocket format”, as Stefano Stoll puts it. In “Almerisa”, her longest-running series, a young Bosnian girl photographed in 1994, aged five, in a refugee center in Leiden, returns over the years, always seated on the same chair. At first, her feet don’t reach the floor. The final portrait, taken in 2024, is shown here for the first time. In the guild’s historic hall, the video “Marianna (The Fairy Doll)” follows a 10-year-old girl repeating her audition for ballet school under her teacher’s sharp instructions, in Russian. A hard school.

Above, visitors climb to the attic of the Musée historique, ordinarily closed to the public, for “Shades of Time 2.0”. “Twenty-five years ago, we were all captivated by this installation”, Stefano Stoll recalls. Annelies Štrba, born in 1947 in Zug, runs through four generations of her family: the house at Melide on Lake Lugano, sleeping children, the kitchen, then the places marked by disaster where her travels led her, Chernobyl, Hiroshima, Kobe. The book, published in 1997 by Lars Müller, became a landmark. In 2020, the artist re-edited the whole sequence digitally, with sound, the old-fashioned way, image after image. It brings to mind Nan Goldin’s The Ballad of Sexual Dependency , relocated to the shores of Ticino: the same hypnotic scroll, the same music holding lives together, and the same tenderness for ordinary days. The slideshow has never before been shown in French-speaking Switzerland (the Röstigraben dies hard). “It’s also wonderful to be able to show this to a generation that’s starting to get hooked on artificial intelligence”, the director adds.

A major figure of the Mexican scene, who represented his country at the Venice Biennale in 2017, Carlos Amorales “isn’t really into photography”, Stefano Stoll admits, having met him on every visit to Mexico City. Except in 1996. As a student in Amsterdam, he invented Los Amorales , a lucha libre alter ego wearing a mask cast from his own face, in a culture where the mask is sacred: “a wrestler never removes his mask, on pain of losing his entire career”, the director notes. Long reluctant to reopen that chapter, the artist gave in for the 30th anniversary. During a month-long residency at La Becque, he selected 150 slides out of hundreds and animated them with artificial intelligence: his girlfriend at the time, the bouts, his own family. At the Théâtre Oriental, a mosaic of raw photographs answers the film. On one side, memory as it was; on the other, as a machine dreams it. Poignant. Artist and father, Carlos Amorales delivers a self-portrait thirty years apart, “a time trip through today’s technology”, says Stefano Stoll. The biennial has thought of everything, down to a label modeled on allergen warnings: “May contain traces of AI”.

Another liturgy: football. At the Cinéma Astor, Zidane: A 21st Century Portrait plays on loop, free of charge. On April 23, 2005, Douglas Gordon and Philippe Parreno trained 17 cameras on the Real Madrid number 5 as he faced Villarreal, from kickoff to the final red card, set to a score by Mogwai. “Football is something that unites nations and families, and just as much divides nations and families”, Stefano Stoll notes, having brought in amateur football media so that sports fans and art lovers could share the same stand. Another video worth a look: at the church of Sainte-Claire, a small screen in a large nave is all Ange Leccia needs to slow down John Travolta in Saturday Night Fever and swap the Bee Gees for Eartha Kitt. “I still felt I was missing something with a bit of grit to it”, the director of Images Vevey admits. On Rue d’Italie, Erika Stucky, queen of jazz-inflected yodel, unveils 44 years of photographs projected behind her at concerts, her blood family and her musical family alike, starting with her first Instamatic snapshot: her parents, nudists. Surprise concerts at 1:13 p.m. and 3:15 p.m. during opening weekend. “She asked us to find her a snow shovel”, Stefano Stoll notes, for the sound effects.

No family escapes grief, says a Chinese proverb Stefano Stoll has made his own. At the Jardin de l’Oyonne, on Quai Roussy, Deanna Dikeman says goodbye, for 27 years running. In 1991, leaving her parents’ home in Sioux City, Iowa, the American photographer shot their wave from her car. The gesture became a ritual. Seasons turn, the photographer’s son grows from a car seat to the driver’s seat, the father disappears from the frame in 2009, days after his 91st birthday, the mother carries on alone, then waves from the doorway of an assisted-living facility, until her death in October 2017. The final photograph: the empty driveway. “For the first time in my life, no one was waving back at me”, Deanna Dikeman writes. The staging, one of a kind, unrolls the chronology, goodbye after goodbye. A crowd favorite in 2022, the installation returns with exactly the same structure, simply relocated to a different garden. Stefano Stoll hopes visitors will say to themselves, “I’ve seen this before, but it wasn’t here, not like this”. Déjà vu, yes, but the same lump in the throat.

Another grief, another scale. Erik Kessels, who once filled a Vevey church with 350,000 images, returns with a single one. That of his sister Susan, struck by a car at nine, when he was 11: the last photograph his parents could find of her, taken in an amusement park. “One Image” spreads unlabeled through the shop windows of Vevey, on billboards, in the press, and explains itself in only one place, on the façade of the Salle del Castillo. A blow to the chest. On Place de l’Hôtel de Ville, Sunil Gupta stages a demonstration: the London marches of 1985 to 1995 against Section 28, the 1988 law that barred schools from presenting homosexuality as a “pretended family relationship” (Margaret Thatcher, an uninvited guest at two exhibitions). At the Salle del Castillo, “Lovers, Revisited”, made with his husband Charan Singh, shows queer couples at home. “Does a gay couple at home make a family? You all have your own answer, but the fact remains it’s still far from a given”, Stefano Stoll observes.

At the Musée Jenisch, which brings together the Grand Prix laureates, Amandine Marchand, in charge of Éditions Images Vevey, leads visitors into an unusual shop. “Undercover Pleasures” takes its name from the sex shop Pacifico Silano’s parents ran in New Jersey when he was a teenager. The American artist, born in 1986 and awarded a special mention, evokes its interior and builds collages from gay erotic magazines of the 1970s and 1980s, pages simply laid one over the other. It all starts from an absence: his uncle, who died of AIDS, erased from the family albums by shame. “Growing up, I only had one Polaroid of my uncle”, Pacifico Silano told BOMB magazine in 2024. The installation also honors his mother, devoted to her own. The family album gets its torn-out pages back. Same museum, another lineage of men: Abdulhamid Kircher, a Grand Prix laureate, studies Turkish oil wrestlers, a tradition dating to the 14th century and practiced within his father’s family, caught between virility and tenderness. Stacy Kranitz, winner of the Book Prize, sets nearly 20 years of photographs of Appalachia against the archives that built the region’s poor reputation ( read our dedicated article ).

Objects, too, have their family stories. Facing the lake, near the Alimentarium, once Nestlé’s headquarters, Tokuko Ushioda lines up eight diptychs, the fridge closed, the fridge open, photographed in Tokyo households between 1981 and 1995. Brillat-Savarin, appliance edition. “Tell me how you keep your fridge, tell me what you eat, and I’ll tell you what kind of family you are”, Stefano Stoll jokes, throat lozenges in his pocket to save his voice before singing that same evening. “It’s one of the last places you show to friends.” Mark Wallinger, by contrast, isolates. Inside a former fast-food outlet (“not Starbucks, Subway”, the director corrects), six anonymous city dwellers turn in circles in front of a large mirror. “You can have 1,000 people walking down the Champs-Élysées, and you still have 1,000 isolated individuals”, Stefano Stoll observes.

Last stop, the Salle del Castillo. JR, whose monumental 2010 and 2012 projects helped Images Vevey “take off”, in Stefano Stoll’s words, marks the 15th anniversary of “Inside Out” here. Vevey was one of the project’s first international stops: 5,200 portraits shot in three weeks, back in 2012. Two cubes face each other. In the first, the faces of 2012; in the second, those of 2026, taken that very morning in a mobile photo booth and pasted up as fast as they came in by the crew. Visitors look for someone, maybe Valérie, and find an artist, a neighbor, an elected official, or themselves 15 years younger. “You are the ones who pushed us to become who we are”, Stefano Stoll says, before concluding, in front of the still-fresh posters: “Family is you.”
Images Vevey Biennial, “We are family!,” 10th edition, September 5–27, 2026, Vevey (Switzerland). Some fifty projects, free of charge; indoor exhibitions open daily from 11 a.m. to 7 p.m.
